title: The New Pump-House, about 1885 (rough draft)
method: Rough draft, modeled with Claude for Chris Busse from curated parts in tools/stations/pump_house.py: outline from OpenStreetMap; levels from the 2019 schematic design study; machinery from The American Engineer (1884); rooms from the 2002 National Register nomination and HAER VA-34. Every part names its sources and how it is known.
about: Richmond's New Pump-House, 1881-83, by Col. Wilfred Emory Cutshaw: canal water turned three turbines that drove nine pumps, lifting drinking water to the Byrd Park reservoir; an open-air pavilion over the machines held dances and pleasure parties.

epochs.title: The New Pump-House at work
epochs.note: The original Ramsay machinery, two years in service; the pavilion still open.

features.name: The New Pump-House: west wing
features.note: Random-ashlar granite from the site and James Netherwood's quarries, built 1881-83 by Col. Wilfred Emory Cutshaw, city engineer (NRHP 2002). Outline from OpenStreetMap; wall thickness approximate. Each end is a cross-gabled wing with lancet windows, a steep slate roof and pinnacled gables; the upper floor held the gentlemen's powder room and offices, and a stair at the south corner (NRHP 2002). The wing roof's height is scaled from HAER VA-34-1 (approximate).

features.note: Tail water in the wheel pit, 20 ft below the forebay (The American Engineer, 1884). Its place in the room is approximate: no plan of the room with the machines was found that can be scaled.

features.name: The New Pump-House: diffuser
features.note: A large cast-iron diffuser below the wheel "delivers the water into the tail-race with the least possible loss" (The American Engineer, 1884). Shape approximate.

features.name: The New Pump-House: turbine wheel 1
features.note: A partial vertical turbine of the outward-flow (Fourneyron) type, all iron, 21 ft inside and 28 ft outside; water under a 20-ft head entered through its center into a guide chamber that turned it onto about a quarter of the buckets. The American Engineer, December 26, 1884: designed by the late Prof. Charles A. Smith, built and erected by H. A. Ramsay (Ramsay Engineering Works, Baltimore) under contract with Col. W. E. Cutshaw. Bolling (1900) gives 23 1/2 ft. Replaced in 1891 by geared Leffel wheels (NRHP 2002). Its place in the room is approximate: no plan of the room with the machines was found that can be scaled.

features.name: The New Pump-House: penstock 1
features.note: An iron penstock 5 ft in diameter, from the forebay through the north wall into the wheel's center (The American Engineer, 1884); three openings in the north wall (NRHP 2002; HAER VA-34-5). Drawn level and square; in the engraving it drops to the wheel on a slant. Its place in the room is approximate: no plan of the room with the machines was found that can be scaled.

features.name: The New Pump-House: penstock 1
features.note: The penstock's elbow into the wheel's center (The American Engineer, 1884). Its place in the room is approximate: no plan of the room with the machines was found that can be scaled.

features.name: The New Pump-House: head gate 1
features.note: A sluice gate 6 ft by 6 ft at the penstock's head, worked by a hydraulic cylinder 10 in in diameter (The American Engineer, 1884). Frame drawn as a block; place approximate.

features.name: The New Pump-House: head gate 1
features.note: The gate's hydraulic cylinder, 10 in (The American Engineer, 1884).

features.name: The New Pump-House: tailrace 1
features.note: A tunnel under the stone walkway carried the spent water out to the canal on the south side (NRHP 2002; Friends of Pump House tour). Number, size and line approximate: one per wheel is assumed.

features.name: The New Pump-House: shaft 1
features.note: A wrought-iron shaft 12 in in diameter, keyed to the wheel, with three cranks of 36-in throw set 120 deg apart (The American Engineer, 1884). Its place in the room is approximate: no plan of the room with the machines was found that can be scaled.

features.name: The New Pump-House: pump 1
features.note: One of nine vertical single-acting plunger pumps: a plunger 14 in in diameter in a chamber 36 in across, with double-beat Cornish valves of 20 in (The American Engineer, 1884); stroke 6 ft (NRHP 2002). Twelve million gallons a day for the nine against a head of 175 ft (The American Engineer). Its place in the room is approximate: no plan of the room with the machines was found that can be scaled.

features.name: The New Pump-House: pavilion floor
features.note: The open-air pavilion over the machine room, 3,392 sq ft (Quinn Evans plan): a painted pine floor, a Gothic arcade of six Tudor arches each side on seven cast-iron columns, the two end arches narrower, with railings of zinc-coated tin; a flat ceiling on wooden trusses. Enclosed with glass in 1899 because rain came through the floor onto the machinery (NRHP 2002). Level from the 2019 study.

features.name: The New Pump-House: roof
features.note: A steep slate roof with rows of imbrication and iron cresting on the ridge, on large wooden trusses (NRHP 2002). Ridge at the 2019 study's 46 ft; pitch approximate. Lifted off in the cutaway, so the dance floor shows.

features.name: Pump House Canal (the forebay)
features.note: Drawn as its surface only. The forebay: the Pump House Canal, turned off above the Three Mile Locks and dammed at the east end of the house; its waterline level with the walkway round the north front (NRHP 2002). The channel's banks are today's lidar (3DEP); its 1885 level is inferred, not measured.

features.name: Pump House Canal (the forebay)

features.name: Pump House Canal: the dam
features.note: The forebay was dammed off at the far east side of the building (NRHP 2002). Its line and form are approximate; the 1924 hydroelectric station stands on it today.

features.name: James River and Kanawha Canal, below the locks
features.note: The canal's lower ("Richmond") level, below the Three Mile Locks, where the tailraces ran out and the water went on to the mills downtown (NRHP 2002; Bolling 1900). Its 1885 level here is the forebay's less the 20-ft fall (approximate). The channel's banks are today's lidar (3DEP); its 1885 level is inferred, not measured.
